site_tour.title: Kendall Interactive Site Tour
site_tour.description: A comprehensive ninety-second walkthrough of Kendall's interactive map, analysis tools, and statistical safeguards.

steps.title: Welcome to Kendall
steps.text: Welcome to Kendall. We are glad you are here. This interactive scientific explorer lets you investigate twenty-five years of continuous NASA satellite and reanalysis observations across planet Earth.

steps.title: Variable Picker
steps.text: Use the dataset bar to switch across atmospheric and terrestrial variables, including rainfall, temperature, soil moisture, evaporation, and wildfire smoke.

steps.title: Point vs Region Analysis
steps.text: Switch between Point mode to inspect single grid cells and Region mode to draw custom bounding boxes with area-weighted spatial aggregation.

steps.title: 25-Year Anomaly Trajectory
steps.text: The time series chart displays monthly anomalies from the long-term climatology, showing the raw trajectory, a twelve-month rolling average, and Sen's slope line.

steps.title: The Verdict Card
steps.text: The Verdict Card evaluates whether an apparent change is genuine or just statistical noise, adjusting strictly for serial autocorrelation.

steps.title: Three Verdict States
steps.text: A location is classified into one of three rigorous states: significant trend with p under five percent, trending but not yet significant, or no trend.

steps.title: Confidence Interval and P-Value
steps.text: The ninety-five percent confidence interval gives the probable range of the rate, while the p-value measures the probability of observing this pattern by random chance.

steps.title: The Detectability Clock
steps.text: The Detectability Clock reveals how many years of continuous observation are needed before a trend cleanly emerges from natural climate noise.

steps.title: Planetary Lineup
steps.text: The Planetary Lineup compares all variables simultaneously at your pinned location, checking whether shifts in rain, temperature, and soil align coherently.

steps.title: Period and Season Filters
steps.text: Slice the record into historical eras like pre-twenty-fourteen versus post-twenty-fourteen, or isolate individual seasons like summer or winter.

steps.title: Monthly Timeline Scrubber
steps.text: Drag the scrubber timeline to step through every single month from June two thousand to September twenty twenty-five, watching global anomalies evolve.

steps.title: Globe and Flat Projections
steps.text: Toggle effortlessly between a realistic three-dimensional orthographic globe and a flat Mercator projection with smooth camera interpolation.

steps.title: Analysis Choices Counter
steps.text: The looks counter tracks your exploratory choices. Searching through multiple combinations increases false positive risk, reminding us to remain skeptical.

steps.title: Sources, Caveats and Curiosity
steps.text: Every calculation adheres to open science standards, citing official NASA missions and stating all instrument limits clearly. Thank you for exploring planet Earth with us, and stay curious.

case_amazon.title: Amazon Basin: Drought or Sensor Break?
case_amazon.description: Investigate whether dramatic Amazon drying reflects a genuine shift or a 2014 satellite sensor discontinuity.

steps.title: Amazon Basin: The Drought Puzzle
steps.text: We travel to the central Amazon Basin. This vast rainforest region has experienced extreme droughts and major fire events over recent decades.

steps.title: Precipitation Trajectory
steps.text: Over twenty-five years, monthly rainfall anomalies show a steep drying slope of -11.96 millimeters per month per decade. An anomaly is a departure from the long-term seasonal average, while a trend measures the steady rate of change over time.

steps.title: Statistical Significance
steps.text: The autocorrelation-aware p-value is 0.0194. A p-value is the probability that random chance produced this pattern. Because p is under zero point zero five, statisticians classify this full-record trend as significant.

steps.title: Confidence Interval
steps.text: The ninety-five percent confidence interval ranges from -22.15 to -1.75 millimeters per decade. A confidence interval gives the estimated range that holds the true underlying rate with ninety-five percent certainty.

steps.title: The 2014 Sensor Transition
steps.text: In early twenty-fourteen, NASA transitioned primary satellites from TRMM to GPM. A step change is an abrupt jump in the data baseline. Before twenty-fourteen the slope was weakly positive, but afterwards it flipped deeply negative.

steps.title: Cross-Dataset Agreement
steps.text: Independent GLDAS reanalysis also shows sharp post-twenty-fourteen drying. However, neither sub-period is statistically significant on its own, showing how sensitive trend estimates can be to the observation window.

steps.title: What This Does Not Mean
steps.text: Crucially, a mathematical trend does not establish physical causation. This signal is not proven to be caused exclusively by local deforestation; historic El Niño drought episodes in twenty-fifteen and twenty-twenty-three heavily shape this record.

case_sahel.title: Sahel Corridor: Greening Recovery Debate
case_sahel.description: Examine whether rainfall recovery in the African Sahel reaches true statistical significance.

steps.title: African Sahel: The Greening Debate
steps.text: We shift our focus to the African Sahel corridor, a semi-arid zone between the Sahara desert and tropical savannas that experienced historic twentieth-century droughts.

steps.title: Modest IMERG Upward Slope
steps.text: IMERG satellite precipitation indicates a modest upward slope of 0.32 millimeters per month per decade. Popular stories often describe this as a permanent greening recovery.

steps.title: Not Yet Significant
steps.text: When we adjust for temporal autocorrelation, the p-value is 0.36. Because p is well above zero point zero five, this result is not yet statistically significant; random year-to-year swings readily explain it.

steps.title: Detectability Window
steps.text: The Detectability Clock indicates that rainfall noise across the Sahel is so high that more than twenty-five years of observation are required before a subtle trend can be confirmed.

steps.title: Dataset Disagreement
steps.text: By contrast, GLDAS reanalysis estimates a steeper rate of 0.73 millimeters per month per decade, which reaches statistical significance at p equals 0.02. Disagreements between models and satellites urge caution.

steps.title: What This Does Not Mean
steps.text: What this does not mean: a modest positive trend is not proven to be a permanent climate recovery; severe annual precipitation deficits still occur regularly across the Sahel.

case_tibet.title: Tibetan Plateau: High-Mountain Warming Hotspot
case_tibet.description: Explore the rapid, statistically indisputable thermal amplification across High-Mountain Asia.

steps.title: Tibetan Plateau: High-Mountain Warming
steps.text: Next, we fly to the high Tibetan Plateau and the Himalayas, known as the Third Pole and the vital water tower of Asia.

steps.title: Intense Thermal Amplification
steps.text: Two-meter air temperature reveals an intense warming slope of 2.75 degrees Celsius per decade. This represents the strongest sustained thermal signal in the dataset.

steps.title: Decisive Significance
steps.text: The autocorrelation-aware p-value is less than zero point zero zero zero one, and it comfortably survives planetary False Discovery Rate control. Chance alone cannot account for this warming.

steps.title: Consistent Confidence Interval
steps.text: The ninety-five percent confidence interval spans from 2.12 to 3.37 degrees Celsius per decade. Both bounds remain deeply positive.

steps.title: Rapid Emergence
steps.text: The Detectability Clock shows this thermal signal was already detectable after just five years of observation, reflecting the high signal-to-noise ratio of high-altitude warming.

steps.title: What This Does Not Mean
steps.text: What this does not mean: regional gridded reanalysis does not capture microclimates in narrow mountain valleys, where local topography and glacier winds create distinct conditions.

case_canada.title: Central Canada: Summer Wildfire Smoke Surge
case_canada.description: Unmask how seasonal slicing reveals intense summer smoke trends invisible in full-year averages.

steps.title: Central Canada: Wildfire Smoke Surge
steps.text: Our final case takes us to central Canada's boreal forests, examining MERRA-2 aerosol optical depth from atmospheric wildfire smoke.

steps.title: Full-Year Averaging Dilutes the Signal
steps.text: Averaged across all twelve calendar months, aerosol optical depth shows only a tiny slope of 0.013 per decade, hiding major fire events beneath winter quiet.

steps.title: Seasonal Slicing Unmasks the Surge
steps.text: Isolating the summer smoke season of June, July, and August reveals a sharper slope of 0.04 per decade, highlighting the value of seasonal filtering.

steps.title: Episodic Megafire Summers
steps.text: The trajectory shows massive spikes in twenty-twenty-one, twenty-twenty-three, and twenty-twenty-five, when unprecedented boreal megafires blanketed North America in smoke.

steps.title: Trending but Not Yet Significant
steps.text: At this individual grid cell, the autocorrelation-aware p-value is 0.09. It is classified as trending but not yet significant at the strict five percent threshold.

steps.title: What This Does Not Mean
steps.text: What this does not mean: wildfire smoke occurs in acute pulses and is not proven to follow a smooth linear progression; intermittent ignition weather drives each extreme season.
